name: Resection Planning and Margins
title: Resection Planning and Margins
answer: Resection planning and margins covers the preoperative and intraoperative work of deciding how much tissue to remove around a tumor or lesion and how to confirm that the removed specimen has an adequate margin. It includes image review, tumor segmentation, definition of target volumes, avoidance of critical structures, and the communication of margin goals to the surgical team. In robotic and navigation assisted surgery, the scope also includes tracking instruments, overlaying planned boundaries on the live field, and linking the resected specimen back to the planned margin. The work sits inside surgical robotics and navigation, part of the broader AI physician field.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Resection planning and margins covers the preoperative and intraoperative work of deciding how much tissue to remove around a tumor or lesion and how to confirm that the removed specimen has an adequate margin. It includes image review, tumor segmentation, definition of target volumes, avoidance of critical structures, and the communication of margin goals to the surgical team. In robotic and navigation assisted surgery, the scope also includes tracking instruments, overlaying planned boundaries on the live field, and linking the resected specimen back to the planned margin. The work sits inside surgical robotics and navigation, part of the broader AI physician field.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on preoperative imaging from CT, MRI, ultrasound, and sometimes PET, stored in DICOM format and managed through PACS. Planning stations use segmentation and 3D reconstruction software, often with GPU acceleration, to turn those images into patient specific anatomy and target volumes. In the operating room, the same plan is loaded onto a navigation system or robotic console, where optical or electromagnetic tracking follows instruments and patient position. Displays, head mounted devices, and robot arms then present the plan in relation to the live surgical field, with compute either on premises or in a controlled cloud environment.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The method starts with image acquisition and segmentation, where a model or a human expert outlines the tumor, organs at risk, and relevant vessels or nerves. Registration aligns those preoperative images to the patient and to the tracking system, and a virtual resection shows what would remain if the planned boundary were followed. During surgery, navigation updates the overlay as tissue moves, and the surgeon may send tissue for frozen section or other intraoperative pathology to check the margin. AI can assist with segmentation, margin classification, or uncertainty estimates, but the plan and the final decision remain with the clinical team.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in this area turn on patient consent, data provenance, device regulation, and clear lines of responsibility when a margin is missed or healthy tissue is removed. Training images and surgical videos carry privacy and licensing constraints, so provenance, de identification, and permitted use are documented. The site tracks 6 active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies, which shows that clinical AI tools can face serious legal exposure. Audit trails, version control, validation records, and human oversight are part of the governance package, and the operating surgeon remains accountable for the resection.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The horizon points toward tighter integration of imaging, pathology, and robotics, with real time margin assessment using fluorescence, Raman spectroscopy, or advanced microscopy feeding back into the navigation display. AI models are likely to move from preoperative segmentation toward intraoperative decision support, including predictions of close or positive margins and alerts for critical structures. Digital twins and patient specific simulation may let teams rehearse a resection before entering the operating room, while federated learning could allow multi site training without moving patient data. Regulatory pathways and reimbursement will shape how quickly these tools reach routine practice, and the field will need consistent ways to measure margin accuracy and clinical benefit.
